ADU218 hardware watchdog + port-write verification
=================================================
Device: Ontrak ADU218, USB 0a07:00da
Witness: SDM4065A s/n SDM46A0CA00021 fw 0.0.0.20, on K0
Wiring: K0 load side -> DMM leads only. No load current.

initial: PK=000 WD=0 DB=1

=== MKddd whole-port write ===
# Only K0 is instrumented, so the DMM witnesses bit 0 while PK
# reports the whole port. MK001 sets K0 alone.
MK001  (K0 only  ) -> PK=001 RPK0=1  DMM: 6.1391 ohm (CLOSED)
MK000  (all off  ) -> PK=000 RPK0=0  DMM: overload sentinel (OPEN)

=== event counters (inputs unwired, so nothing should count) ===
RE0 twice: 00000 then 00000   (REn reads without clearing)
RC0 (read+clear): 00000
RE0 after RC0:    00000

=== DBn de-bounce round trip ===
# 0 = 10 ms, 1 = 1 ms (power-on default), 2 = 100 us
DB0 -> DB reads 0
DB2 -> DB reads 2
DB1 -> DB reads 1
restored to power-on default; was '1', now '1'

=== THE WATCHDOG: does a timeout really open the relays? ===
# Sequence: close K0, confirm with the DMM, arm WD1 (1 s), then go
# SILENT. Any command - even an invalid one - refeeds the timer, so
# polling would prevent the very timeout being tested.
K0 closed:  RPK0=1  DMM: 6.1390 ohm (CLOSED)
WD1 armed:  WD=1   <- reading WD refed the timer; clock restarts now
staying silent for 3.0 s (timeout is 1 s)...
after 3.7 s of ADU218 silence:            <- SEE CORRECTION BELOW: this figure
                                             is sleep(3.0) plus the DMM read
                                             latency, NOT the trip time
  DMM (independent, feeds nothing): overload sentinel (OPEN)
  RPK0=0  PK=000
  WD=0   <- manual says a timeout also resets this to 0

=== control: does the watchdog leave relays alone while fed? ===
K0 closed and WD1 armed: RPK0=1 DMM: 6.1393 ohm (CLOSED)
feeding the timer with PK every 0.3 s for 3.0 s...
after 3.1 s of being fed:
  RPK0=1  WD=1  DMM: 6.1392 ohm (CLOSED)
  (if RPK0=1 and WD=1 here, the watchdog only fires on real silence)

restored: WD=0 PK=000 DB=1

CORRECTION: the "3.7 s" above is not a trip time
------------------------------------------------
This capture reports "after 3.7 s of ADU218 silence: OPEN". That number is
sleep(3.0) plus the latency of the DMM read that followed it - an upper bound
on when the trip was OBSERVED, not a measurement of when it FIRED. The relay
opened somewhere inside an unobserved window. This file timed the observation
and labelled it the timeout.

The error is worth keeping on the record because of what it invited: read as a
trip time, 3.7 s against a documented 1 s suggests the interval is ~3.7x its
label and cannot be trusted, which would make every WD interval a thing to
characterise rather than rely on. A reviewer drew exactly that conclusion from
this line.

Measured properly by bisection in watchdog_trip.txt (stay silent for exactly T,
then one RPK0 read that terminates the window): still closed at 0.90 s, open by
1.10 s, so the WD1 trip is in (0.90, 1.10] s. That is the documented 1 s. There
is no timing anomaly, and the design consequences below do not depend on one:
they follow from arming coupling relay state to call frequency, which is
unaffected.

INTERPRETATION
--------------
The watchdog works as documented, and the control case is what makes that
claim safe to rely on: a fed timer left K0 closed for 3.1 s while an unfed one
opened it, so the relay drop is caused by silence and not by arming WD1.

Both halves were witnessed by the DMM, which sits on a different bus and
therefore cannot feed the ADU218 by being read. That matters: RPK0 is the
device reporting on itself, and a firmware that lied about relay state would
lie consistently. The overload sentinel is independent evidence the contact
physically opened.

Why this is more than a device feature
--------------------------------------
KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md N-1 states the honest position that "a software deadman
cannot guarantee an output goes off", and ROADMAP.md's "Hardware interlock for
unattended runs" is open work waiting on a GPIO e-stop button ordered
2026-08-19. This device is a second, independent answer to the same problem:
the relay opens because the HOST WENT QUIET, with no benchctrl process, no
GPIO, and no kernel driver involved in the decision. A wedged agent, a killed
process, an unplugged USB cable and a panicking kernel all produce the same
silence, and all therefore de-energise the load.

The design consequences are not obvious, so they are written down rather than
inferred later:

1. Arming the watchdog makes EVERY relay's state depend on call frequency. A
   driver that arms it and then blocks for longer than the interval - one
   pyvisa call to another instrument would do it - silently opens the load it
   was told to hold closed. So WD must never be armed implicitly, and the
   driver must not offer a "keep alive" thread that hides the coupling.

2. WD1 (1 s, confirmed in watchdog_trip.txt) is too tight for a general-purpose
   bench. The ladder is bounded and documented: WD0=off, WD1=1 s, WD2=10 s,
   WD3=1 min, and n is constrained to 0..3 - there is no WD4 and no custom
   interval, so 1 min is the longest available. WD3 is the only setting a run
   loop can plausibly meet without a dedicated feeder. Note WDn both sets the
   interval and arms in one command; there is no separate arm step.

3. There is no way to distinguish "the watchdog fired" from "someone opened the
   relays" by reading relay state alone - but WD resetting itself to 0 IS a
   distinguishable trace, and it is the only one. Polling WD is how a host
   learns a timeout happened (the manual says as much in section 6d). That
   read must be recorded in the run's event stream, because a fired interlock
   that is not in the artifact bundle is a gap in the audit trail.

   BUT the trace is weaker than it looks, and the qualification matters: WD=0
   means BOTH "timed out" and "never enabled". It is only interpretable against
   a driver-held expected value, so a driver restart loses the ability to
   interpret it - the first WD read after a restart is ambiguous by
   construction. Consequences: the driver must hold the armed-state itself and
   compare, and it should write WD0 explicitly at open() unless it is using the
   watchdog, so that later reads have a known starting point rather than an
   inherited one.

4. The feed-vs-timeout coupling is exactly the failure mode described in
   memory as the "inert governor" trap: a watchdog nobody feeds looks identical
   to a watchdog that works, until the day it should have fired. A test must
   assert the LADDER - fed stays closed, unfed opens - against a synthetic
   clock, not just that WD1 is accepted.

5. A status poller silently disables the watchdog. Any command refeeds the
   timer, so a health-check loop that reads PK on a timer keeps the deadman fed
   no matter how wedged the control path is - the exact inert-governor shape
   from memory, and demonstrated by the control case above, which held the
   relay closed using nothing but PK. So if the watchdog is the safety
   mechanism, the feed must live on the CONTROL path and nowhere else, and the
   driver must not expose a background feeder at all. A benchctrl dashboard
   polling device state would be enough to neuter it.
